facts.statement: Icadyptes was an extinct genus of giant penguins that lived in the Late Eocene tropics of South America.
facts.quote: Icadyptes is an extinct genus of giant penguins from the Late Eocene tropics of South America.

facts.statement: Icadyptes possessed an exceptionally long, spear-like beak that resembled that of a heron.
facts.quote: It had an exceptionally long spear-like beak resembling that of a heron.

facts.statement: The estimated standing height of Icadyptes is 1.5 meters.
facts.quote: standing height of Icadyptes is estimated at 1.5 m.

facts.statement: A well-preserved skeleton of Icadyptes was found on the southern coast of Peru alongside the early Eocene species Perudyptes devriesi.
facts.quote: Its well-preserved Fossil skeleton was found on the southern coast of Peru together with an early Eocene species, Perudyptes devriesi

facts.statement: The fossils were discovered by the team of North Carolina State University paleontologist Dr. Julia Clarke.
facts.quote: by the team of North Carolina State University palaeontologist Dr. Julia Clarke

facts.statement: Fossils of Icadyptes salasi and Perudyptes devriesi were discovered in 2005 by a team of Peruvian paleontologists.
facts.quote: Los fósiles de Icadyptes salasi y Perudyptes devriesi fueron descubiertos en 2005 por un equipo de paleontólogos peruanos.

facts.statement: Icadyptes salasi stood about 150 cm tall and was found in the desert coasts of the Ica region in southern Peru.
facts.quote: Medía unos 150 cm de altura y fue hallado en las costas desérticas de Ica, región al sur del país.

facts.statement: The species name 'salasi' honors the noted Peruvian paleontologist Rodolfo Salas.
facts.quote: Ica por la región donde el fósil fue encontrado, dyptes que en griego significa nadador y salasi en honor al reconocido paleontólogo peruano Rodolfo Salas.

facts.statement: The genus name combines 'Ica', the region where the fossil was found, and 'dyptes', the Greek word for diver.
facts.quote: Ica por la región donde el fósil fue encontrado, dyptes que en griego significa nadador

facts.statement: Because Icadyptes salasi lived in warm Peru, penguins must have adapted to warm climates approximately 30 million years earlier than previously thought.
facts.quote: Since Icadyptes salasi lived in Peru during a period of great warmth, penguins must have adapted to warm climates around 30 million years earlier than previously believed.

facts.statement: Icadyptes salasi is classified in the family Spheniscidae and the subfamily Palaeeudyptinae.
facts.quote: regnum: Animalia phylum: Chordata classis: Aves ordo: Sphenisciformes familia: Spheniscidae subfamilia: †Palaeeudyptinae genus: Icadyptes species: I. salasi

facts.statement: Icadyptes salasi is an extinct species of sphenisciform bird belonging to the family Spheniscidae.
facts.quote: Icadyptes salasi es una especie extinta de ave esfenisciforme de la familia Spheniscidae

facts.statement: The fossil range of Icadyptes spans the Late Eocene, specifically the Divisaderan to Tinguirirican stages.
Icadyptes lived between 37.71 and 33.9 million years ago during the Priabonian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Priabonian to Priabonian (37.71 to 33.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: Researchers believe the long, pointed beak of Icadyptes may represent the ancestral shape for all penguins.
facts.quote: The researchers who discovered the penguins believe the long, pointed beaks are the likely ancestral shape for all penguins.

facts.statement: Today, only a few penguin species, such as the African and Galapagos penguins, prefer the warm climates that Icadyptes inhabited.
facts.quote: Only a few modern-day penguins, such as the African and Galapagos penguins prefer such a balmy climate.

facts.statement: It is debated whether penguins evolved near the poles and migrated to the equator only 10 million years ago, as the discovery of Icadyptes suggests an earlier adaptation to warm climates.
facts.quote: Previously, scientists believed that penguins evolved near the poles in Antarctica and New Zealand, and moved closer to the equator around 10 million years ago.
